segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Bell asks two shillings a night for the small room over the arch, and a further sixpence if a man wants a fire, and Captain Farr had taken the room and gone without the fire. He had eleven pounds and a half-pay warrant that would not be answered until the quarter. He had also a landlord who had known his great-uncle and was willing to chalk it up, which is a kind of charity that costs a man more than it saves him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: On Saturday morning he crossed the green to the apothecary's and knocked at the house door beside the shop, and Miss Vane opened it with her sleeves pinned back and flour to the wrist.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: You are thinner.

segments.speaker: Captain Nathaniel Farr
segments.text: You are the first person in this parish to say anything to me that was true. Everyone else has said how glad they are.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: They are glad. They are only glad at a distance, in case it should cost them something.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She had lent him a book once, a Life of Nelson, the summer before he went for a soldier, and he had returned it in the yard of this very house with a corner turned down that she had never afterward been able to smooth flat. Neither of them mentioned it. She wiped her hands and took him through into the shop.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Mr Owen Vane was weighing something small on the counter scale and did not look pleased to be interrupted. When his sister had laid out the business in nine sentences he set the scale down very carefully, as a man does when he wishes to appear calm.

segments.speaker: Mr Owen Vane
segments.text: Judith. Mr Hartwell has an account here. He has had camphor and a black draught off me since Michaelmas and he pays at the quarter, which is more than half the parish does.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: I am not asking you to quarrel with him. I am asking you what is in your book.

segments.speaker: Mr Owen Vane
segments.text: And when it is read out at Winchester with my name on it, whose quarrel will it be then?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he had already reached the shelf. He is exact with dates and numbers, and he cannot bear to be asked a thing he can answer and leave it unanswered. The dispensing book came down, brown leather, ruled in four columns, and he turned to September and ran his thumb along the entries.

segments.speaker: Mr Owen Vane
segments.text: The fourteenth. Fenner, Oakmere. A draught against pain, and a strong one, and I carried it out myself before nine because the boy had gone to Alresford. That is my hand and my initial in the last column.

segments.speaker: Captain Nathaniel Farr
segments.text: The will is dated the fourteenth.

segments.speaker: Mr Owen Vane
segments.text: Then the will was signed some hours after I stood in his bedchamber. He knew me at first. He called me by my father's name, and then he could not get to the end of his own. Not his own name. He tried it twice.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The shop was quiet. Somebody outside dragged a barrow across the cobbles and the noise went off down toward the forge.

segments.speaker: Captain Nathaniel Farr
segments.text: Then that is our proof.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: It is not. It is a village apothecary's book against a gentleman's paper witnessed by two servants, and any attorney in Winchester will say a man may be heavy in the morning and clear by noon. It proves what he was given. It does not prove what he was when the pen was in his hand.

segments.speaker: Captain Nathaniel Farr
segments.text: Then nothing proves it.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: Somebody was in that room. Somebody held the paper for him and put her name under his.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Farr thought of an upstairs window and a hand pressed flat against the glass, and of a woman who had known him since he was seven years old standing there and letting him walk away.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: Mrs Whitlow said nothing to you because she has been told what she is to say. I shall go up to Oakmere on Monday, and I shall take Mr Rowe, and we shall go about the parish alms, and nobody will think anything of it at all.
